title: B-trees: the index almost every database starts with
dek: The B-tree is the most common index there is: primary keys, unique constraints and ordinary indexes in PostgreSQL and MySQL are B-trees, and so are MongoDB's indexes. It keeps keys sorted in a wide, shallow, always-balanced tree whose nodes are the size of a disk page, so any key is a few page reads away, whether you look up one value or a range. In an interview, if you need an index and nothing special applies, a B-tree is the safe answer.

items: A B-tree node holds hundreds of sorted keys and pointers and fills one disk page. Three or four levels reach any of crores of keys.
It stays balanced as rows are inserted and deleted: all leaves sit at the same depth, so every lookup costs about the same few page reads.
Because keys stay sorted, one B-tree serves exact matches, ranges and ORDER BY. That is why it's the default.

body.x: A B-tree is a self-balancing tree that keeps its keys sorted and allows fast searches, inserts and deletes. Unlike a binary tree, where each node has at most two children, a B-tree node can have hundreds. Each node holds an ordered list of keys and, between them, pointers to the children that cover the ranges in between.

body.cap: Each page holds hundreds of keys, so the tree is wide and shallow. Three levels cover crores of names, and the top levels stay in memory.

body.x: Every B-tree follows a few strict rules:

items: All leaf nodes are at the same depth, so no lookup takes longer than another.
Each node (except the root) holds between m/2 and m keys, where m, the order of the tree, is set by how many keys fit in a page.
A node with k keys has exactly k + 1 children: one for the values below the first key, one between each pair of keys, one above the last.
The keys inside a node are kept in sorted order.

body.x: The clever part is how well this matches disks. Each node is sized to fill one page, typically 8 KB in PostgreSQL, so reading a node is exactly one page read. To find the row with id 350, the database reads the root page, perhaps one internal page, and one leaf page: two or three reads, even in a big table.

body.cap: Looking up id 350: the root says 'between 300 and 600', an internal page narrows it to '340 to 360', and the leaf page holds the entry pointing to the row. Three page reads.

body.x: When a leaf fills up, the next insert splits it into two half-full leaves and adds a key for the new leaf to the parent. If the parent fills up, it splits too, and occasionally the split reaches the root, which then gets a new root above it: the tree grows by one level, at the top, for every leaf at once. Deletes merge or rebalance nodes that get too empty. Because growth only happens at the root, all leaves always stay at the same depth.

body.cap: A full leaf receives one more key: it splits into two half-full leaves and the parent gains a key pointing to the new one. The tree stays balanced.

body.x: B-trees are everywhere. PostgreSQL uses them for nearly everything: primary keys, unique constraints and most ordinary indexes. Create this table:

body.label: Two indexes you didn't ask for
body.x:
CREATE TABLE users (
  id     BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  phone  VARCHAR(15) UNIQUE
);
-- PostgreSQL creates two B-tree indexes:
--   users_pkey       on (id)
--   users_phone_key  on (phone)
body.say: Create a users table with an id that is the primary key and a phone number that must be unique. PostgreSQL creates two B-tree indexes automatically: one for the primary key on id, and one for the unique constraint on phone.

body.x: PostgreSQL silently creates two B-tree indexes here: one for the primary key and one to enforce the unique phone number. Keeping keys sorted is what makes the uniqueness check and range queries cheap.

items: MySQL's InnoDB stores the table itself as a B+ tree ordered by primary key (a clustered index), and every secondary index is a B+ tree pointing to primary keys.

MongoDB, despite its document model, also uses B-trees for its indexes (B+ trees, a variant that keeps all entries in the leaves and links the leaves for fast scans). db.users.createIndex({ phone: 1 }) builds a B-tree from phone numbers to documents.

DynamoDB keeps items within a partition sorted by their sort key, which is what makes range queries within a partition efficient. Its storage engine isn't documented in detail and is generally understood to be LSM-style rather than a B-tree; the article 'LSM trees and hash indexes' explains the difference.
They keep keys sorted, so range queries (age > 25, orders this week) and ORDER BY are efficient.
They balance themselves, so performance stays predictable as the table grows.
Their nodes match disk pages, so every step is one page read.
They handle exact matches (phone = '…') and ranges equally well.
They stay balanced under random inserts and deletes, with none of the sudden slowdowns simpler trees suffer when data arrives in an unlucky order.

body.x: If an interviewer asks which index you'd use and the data is ordinary, a B-tree is a safe answer. The article 'Indexes' in Concepts goes further into how databases plan queries around them.

items: Say 'a B-tree index on …' and give the query it serves.
Mention that it serves ranges and sorting too, so one index can cover 'this user's orders, newest first'.
Know that primary keys and unique constraints already come with one.
